alternatives: Lamotrigine: no interaction with lisinopril or atorvastatin; slow titration over 6 to 8 weeks.
Lacosamide: no interaction with lisinopril or atorvastatin; prolongs the PR interval in a dose-dependent way.
Oxcarbazepine: weak CYP3A4 induction at higher doses; hyponatremia risk rises with age.
output.formulary_status: Levetiracetam is on formulary; generic available
interactions: Levetiracetam + lisinopril: no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction; levetiracetam is renally cleared, so its dose follows renal function.
Levetiracetam + atorvastatin: no interaction; levetiracetam neither induces nor inhibits CYP3A4.
Carbamazepine, phenytoin or phenobarbital + atorvastatin: CYP3A4 induction lowers atorvastatin exposure substantially and can cost lipid control.
output.proposed: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily, titrated to 1000 mg twice daily; current medicines lisinopril 10 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime
output.summary: Levetiracetam and lamotrigine have no interaction with lisinopril or atorvastatin; enzyme-inducing antiseizure medicines lower atorvastatin exposure; lacosamide prolongs PR.
warnings: Levetiracetam can cause irritability, low mood or anxiety; ask about psychiatric history before starting.
PR interval on the current ECG is 194 ms: if lacosamide is chosen, repeat the ECG after titration.
Lamotrigine carries a risk of serious rash during titration; follow the titration schedule.

output.query: seizure versus syncope differentiation convulsive syncope older adults

results.finding: Transient loss of consciousness is classified as syncope, epileptic seizure or psychogenic event by history; in syncope, myoclonic jerks are common, usually brief and begin after the fall, and recovery of orientation is rapid, whereas prolonged postictal confusion, an aura and automatisms favor an epileptic seizure.
results.source: Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948 | 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope

results.finding: An elevated serum prolactin measured 10 to 20 minutes after an event is a useful adjunct for separating generalized tonic-clonic or complex partial seizures from psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; it does not separate epileptic seizures from syncope, and a normal level does not exclude a seizure.
results.source: Chen DK, So YT, Fisher RS, Neurology 2005;65:668-675 | Use of serum prolactin in diagnosing epileptic seizures: report of the Therapeutics and Technology Assessment Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology

results.finding: In newly diagnosed focal epilepsy, levetiracetam did not meet non-inferiority to lamotrigine for time to 12-month remission, and lamotrigine was the most cost-effective option.
results.source: Marson A et al., Lancet 2021;397:1363-1374 | The SANAD II study of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of levetiracetam, zonisamide, or lamotrigine for newly diagnosed focal epilepsy: an open-label, non-inferiority, multicentre, phase 4, randomised controlled trial

output.summary: History is the main tool for separating syncope from epileptic seizures (ESC 2018). Postictal prolactin helps against psychogenic events but not against syncope (AAN 2005). Lamotrigine performed best in SANAD II for focal epilepsy.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the events to cardiac syncope: the cardiac work-up is negative and video-EEG recorded habitual events with right temporal onset and no arrhythmia.
Do not implant a pacemaker or loop recorder for these events.
Do not prescribe flecainide, sotalol or other antiarrhythmic drugs for these events.
Do not pursue electrophysiology study or ablation without a documented arrhythmia.
Do not start carbamazepine, phenytoin or phenobarbital without accounting for the induction that lowers atorvastatin exposure.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for no interaction with atorvastatin or lisinopril; avoid enzyme-inducing ASMs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital), which lower atorvastatin exposure.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Tell him and his cardiologist that the events are epileptic seizures, so that the syncope work-up is closed.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, alert, six months of stereotyped events and no feature of infection or encephalitis: lumbar puncture adds nothing.
Elective inpatient assessment with MRI available and no recent head injury, deficit or anticoagulation: CT adds radiation and cannot show the hippocampal sclerosis.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin (focal-onset seizures with impaired awareness and secondary focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic evolution), with right mesial temporal sclerosis and remote cortical injury

differential.diagnosis: Convulsive syncope from a cardiac arrhythmia
differential.key_features: Considered after a slump with jerking and a paternal cardiac death; excluded by the negative Holter, echocardiogram and ECG and by sinus tachycardia without bradycardia or asystole during two recorded habitual seizures.
No postural or emotional trigger, no prodromal pallor or sweating, negative tilt-table test, a 20-minute postictal confusion and habitual events with right temporal ictal onset on video-EEG.
Excluded by video-EEG capture of habitual events with a right temporal ictal correlate; the ED prolactin raised 22 minutes after the convulsive episode also argues against it.
Vascular risk factors, but TIAs cause negative symptoms without aura, automatisms or postictal confusion; the events are electroclinical seizures.
Epigastric aura, deja vu and oroalimentary automatisms with right anterior temporal ictal onset and right hippocampal sclerosis localize to the temporal lobe.

key_clinical_evidence: Stereotyped rising epigastric sensation and deja vu, then impaired awareness with oroalimentary and right-hand automatisms and minutes of postictal confusion, is mesial temporal semiology, not syncope.
The one convulsive episode (leftward head turn, bilateral stiffening and jerking for about 40 seconds, 20 minutes of confusion) was a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, not convulsive syncope.
A normal ECG (PR 194 ms, upper limit of normal), Holter, echocardiogram and tilt-table test leave no cardiac cause; the cardiac work-up was justified but does not itself establish the diagnosis.
Routine EEG shows right anterior temporal sharp-and-slow waves, and video-EEG records two habitual seizures with right anterior temporal onset and sinus tachycardia, no asystole.
MRI shows right hippocampal sclerosis and a remote right temporal pole lesion from the head injury at 38, concordant with the EEG.
The ED prolactin of 48 ng/mL drawn 22 minutes after the convulsive episode argues against a psychogenic event; prolactin does not separate a seizure from syncope.
He takes atorvastatin: enzyme-inducing ASMs would lower its exposure, so lamotrigine or levetiracetam is preferred.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The episode began with his habitual aura, had a leftward head turn and about 40 seconds of bilateral stiffening and jerking, and was followed by 20 minutes of confusion: a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Convulsive syncope causes brief jerks with rapid recovery.
red_herrings.data_point: A convulsive episode after slumping in a chair, attributed by the emergency department to convulsive syncope.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on the convulsive movements and cardiac family history as evidence of cardiogenic syncope; extend and repeat cardiac workup rather than pursuing neurological evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A PR interval of 194 ms is within normal limits (first-degree AV block is above 200 ms) and is not a cause of recurrent blackouts; Holter, tilt-table test and echocardiogram were also negative. It matters only for the choice of lacosamide.
red_herrings.data_point: PR interval 194 ms, at the upper limit of normal, on the 12-lead ECG.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Over-interpret a borderline ECG finding as a potential cardiac cause warranting electrophysiology referral or additional cardiac workup, delaying neurological evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Negative cardiac workup is necessary to exclude syncope when the differential is genuinely open, but it does not establish an alternative diagnosis. The presence of stereotyped temporal-lobe semiology demands EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI regardless of cardiac workup completeness.
red_herrings.data_point: Extensive 8-week prior cardiac workup (ECG, 48-hour Holter, echocardiogram, tilt-table) performed before neurology referral.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Assume that because cardiology completed a thorough workup, a cardiac cause has been excluded and the diagnosis is idiopathic/functional; overlook the epileptic semiology and delay EEG evaluation.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. H is a 55-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a remote closed head injury at age 38, who presents for inpatient neurology evaluation following a 6-month history of recurrent paroxysmal episodes that were initially attributed to vasovagal or cardiac syncope. The episodes began insidiously approximately 6 months ago. They are stereotyped: the patient first notices a vague uncomfortable rising sensation from the epigastrium toward the chest, followed by an intense, brief feeling of deja vu ('I know I've been here before but I know I haven't'). He then loses awareness of his surroundings. His wife, who has witnessed multiple episodes, reports that he stares blankly, makes chewing and lip-smacking movements, and occasionally performs repetitive fumbling motions with his right hand. Episodes last 60-90 seconds on average. Post-ictally, he is confused and fatigued for approximately 5 minutes before returning to full alertness. He reports having no memory of the episode itself.

Approximately 3 months ago, one episode witnessed by his wife began with his usual rising sensation and staring; he then slumped in his chair, his head turned to the left, and he stiffened and had rhythmic jerking of both arms and legs, more marked on the left, for about 40 seconds. He was confused for about 20 minutes afterwards and was taken to the emergency department. Because he had slumped in a chair and his father died of a myocardial infarction, the emergency department attributed the convulsive movements to convulsive syncope and arranged urgent cardiac evaluation. Extensive cardiac workup over the following 8 weeks included a 12-lead ECG, a 48-hour Holter monitor (no arrhythmia), a transthoracic echocardiogram (normal), and a head-up tilt-table test (negative for vasovagal response). All cardiac studies were unrevealing, and cardiology referred him for neurological evaluation. He has had a total of 11 episodes over 6 months. No clear positional or exertional trigger for any episode. No prodromal lightheadedness, diaphoresis, or pallor reported before the deja vu aura. He has self-restricted driving since the second episode. He has not been started on any antiepileptic medication.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue lacerations. No urinary incontinence reported with episodes. His wife describes the one convulsive episode: he slumped in a chair, his head turned to the left, and he stiffened and jerked in all four limbs, more on the left, for about 40 seconds, then was confused for about 20 minutes; she called emergency services.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin performed without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements symmetric and intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive bilaterally (3 mm to 2 mm). Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact in all three divisions bilaterally. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevation symmetric. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait, steady base. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent without word-finding difficulty. Naming and repetition intact. Recalls 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. Mood and affect appropriate. During interview, patient describes episodic spells characterized by a rising epigastric sensation followed by a sense of deja vu lasting 10-20 seconds, then a period of unawareness he cannot recall. Wife present and confirms she has witnessed episodes in which patient stares blankly and performs chewing and lip-smacking movements; episodes last 60-90 seconds and are followed by confusion lasting approximately 5 minutes.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups bilaterally. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception intact in all extremities. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
